All thirteen tests pass, across the four test files.

**What changed in `editor/buffer.py`**

- **`clear_history()`** empties both the undo and redo stacks and leaves the text untouched.
- **`find_all(s)`** scans left to right with the built-in string search, resuming after each match so matches never overlap. An empty search string returns an empty list, since it would otherwise match at every position and loop forever.
- **`replace_all(old, new)`** finds all matches first, then replaces them inside a transaction from right to left so earlier positions are not shifted by length changes. The transaction makes the whole operation one undo step. When there are no matches, the transaction is empty and nothing is recorded.

Beyond the test suite, I checked by hand that overlapping candidates are skipped, that replacements of differing length undo and redo correctly, and that a zero-match call leaves history unchanged.

```
python -m pytest -q
13 passed in 0.04s
```

**Undo architecture**

The codebase uses Approach A, the command pattern, and it has used it since the first commit. That never changed. Every edit is stored as a record of a position plus the old and new text at that position, and undo swaps old for new. The one structural addition along the way was a composite command in the transactions round, which groups a sequence of those records into a single step. That is an extension of the command pattern, not a switch to mementos. I considered the whole-text snapshot you mentioned for transaction rollback and declined it, because inverting the pending edits in reverse gives the same guarantee while keeping memory proportional to edit size and keeping one consistent mechanism throughout.
